content: Individuals with neuromuscular disorders (NMDs) often experience weakened respiratory muscles, which compromises their ability to cough effectively and clear mucus from their lungs. This inability to clear mucus increases their susceptibility to recurrent chest infections and chronic lung disease. Mechanical insufflation-exsufflation (MI-E) is a therapeutic technique designed to enhance cough effectiveness and facilitate mucus clearance in such individuals. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of MI-E in individuals with NMDs. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted on October 7, 2013, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform to identify ongoing trials. Reference lists and conference proceedings were also manually reviewed. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized clinical trials, as well as randomized cross-over trials, that investigated the use of MI-E for airway clearance in individuals with NMDs and respiratory insufficiency. Comparisons were made between MI-E and either no treatment or alternative cough augmentation techniques. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias using standard Cochrane methodology. The primary outcome of interest was mortality during follow-up or at six months. Five studies, involving a total of 105 participants, met the inclusion criteria. All of these studies were short-term, lasting two days or less, and focused on the immediate effects of the interventions. The reports lacked sufficient detail to adequately assess the methods of randomization and allocation concealment. Furthermore, all five studies were at high risk of bias due to the absence of blinding. None of the studies reported on critical outcomes such as mortality, morbidity, quality of life, serious adverse events, or other pre-specified outcomes. One of the included studies was a randomized cross-over trial conducted over two days, where participants received two interventions twice daily in a randomly assigned order, with a reverse cross-over on the second day. The other four studies applied multiple cough augmentation interventions to each participant in a random order. One study reported fatigue as an adverse effect of MI-E, using a visual analogue scale to measure this outcome. Peak cough expiratory flow (PCEF) was the most commonly reported outcome measure, appearing in four of the studies. Based on data from three studies, MI-E may improve PCEF compared to unassisted coughing. However, all interventions, including MI-E, were shown to increase PCEF to the critical threshold required for effective mucus clearance. The studies did not provide clear evidence that MI-E improves cough expiratory flow more effectively than other cough augmentation techniques. In one study, which was at risk of assessor bias, the addition of MI-E to a standard airway clearance regimen with manually assisted cough appeared to reduce treatment time. MI-E was reported to be as well-tolerated as other cough augmentation techniques, based on comfort scores from three studies. The authors concluded that the findings of this review do not provide sufficient evidence to guide clinical practice regarding the use of MI-E. Important shortand long-term outcomes, including adverse effects, were not adequately addressed. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of MI-E in individuals with NMDs. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the safety and efficacy of MI-E in this population.
